P1.evidence: The setter handoff was acknowledged and lightly used — 'from what I saw from the notes, that you're a technical project manager' and 'Kim that you spoke with briefed me a little bit about your situation' — but the notes were not read back, and the framing was the opposite: 'I'm kind of old school and I would love to hear it from you.' No four-part frame and no frame agreement. The open question ran: 'brief me in, like, what's your situation? How can we actually potentially help you with it?'

P2.evidence: The best baseline in the batch on health. Hereditary conditions were properly chased — 'both of your parents, they have diabetes?' followed by 'And their parents, too?' — and current status was tested directly with 'Do you have high blood pressure already?'. The injury probe is exemplary and repeated: 'brief me in, because this is important for us, what's your situation with injuries?', 'Does it also appear in a daily situation?', 'those shots for pain or just like that?', 'does it show up only when you're working out, or you wake up and already have some stiffness?', then a full second pass on the knees — 'when you say what's wrong with the legs?' and 'What do you mean they hurt sometimes?'. Diet was asked and then pressure-tested ('you said you were pretty religious about paleo, what do you actually mean? Like calorie counting?'). Results from current training were confirmed ('and you dropped, like, significantly, yeah?'). Height was confirmed and weight explored; age was volunteered. Training week was only loosely covered — no question about how many days he actually trains. Sleep and energy were never asked, which is the one real gap in an otherwise excellent phase.

P3.evidence: Every check ran, and the back half is the strongest work in the batch. The bridge was direct and repeated when the first answer was thin — 'Let me ask you directly. Why? Why do you want to do it?' and 'What's behind that, yeah? When you're saying it out loud, I want to get ripped, what are the first thoughts that are coming to your mind?'. The future-worth question ran ('when you think about future version of you, version 2.0 of Manny... what would that moment actually be worth to you?'), the impact question ran ('You mentioned you have kids. How old are they?... How do they play into this?'), and it drove all the way to legacy — the prospect's father drunk on the floor, his step-grandfather's amputated leg, wanting to be a healthy grandfather, and refusing to repeat the body-shaming he grew up with. The reflect-back was excellent: 'you feel like you are the one that can actually break this vicious cycle of your family right now.' Two process notes. The aesthetics thread was pushed roughly five minutes past the point the prospect had answered it, which produced pushback — 'if this program is all about just me getting ripped and shredded, then this isn't the right program for me.' And the rep then supplied the why rather than eliciting it: 'I would be leaning towards your health situation with your diabetes.'

P4.evidence: Past attempts were inventoried in detail — paleo, CrossFit, a bulking programme, AI macro tracking — and what happened with each was established, including that CrossFit caused lasting damage and that paleo worked but the numbers drifted back. The root-cause question was well framed: 'You said you've been kind of yo-yoing ups and downs. How do you feel? What's the missing piece that you cannot seem to keep it steady?' The rep then tested the answer with a concrete scenario ('you wake up, life got busy, you didn't go to the gym, so the rest of the day was up... either it's 100% or nothing, yeah?'), which surfaced the all-or-nothing spiral the prospect then described himself. The prospect named his own gap: 'I need to find a way to be able to enjoy life' and 'I need that extra support to get there.' The explicit information-isn't-the-problem line was never run, which barely mattered because this prospect already knows the information.

P5.evidence: The forward-looking question ran early and well — 'if you think about that, about your future and next two, five years, what's the most important thing for you?' — and produced the diabetes, cholesterol and blood pressure answer. The problem is sequencing: the cost-of-inaction material was mostly deployed after the price objection rather than before it, and at that point it backfired. 'How much it's going to cost you when you have diabetes. Or you're injured and you cannot work' was met with a valid rebuttal, and 'we can both agree that doing nothing isn't the best thing for you, right?' got 'Yeah, but you know, I'm not doing nothing. So I told you that I'm at Manny 1.5.' He was right — he runs sub-seven-minute miles and tracks his own A1C. Consequence pressure does not work on a prospect who is already acting, and no line-in-the-sand was attempted.

P6.evidence: Both questions ran cleanly and in order before price: 'If you had the right training, the right nutrition, and real accountability from Trevor, all built around your life, do you agree that it would get you to the Manny 2.0 that we covered?' and 'if we can figure out the details like the investment and everything, are you actually fully committed to showing up and doing the work?'. P6c is partial because the yes came back explicitly conditional — 'if this is something that I can afford and I can do, I'm in' — and the rep treated it as clean and moved straight to price. That condition was the entire call, and forty minutes of price work followed without it ever being explored.

P11.evidence: The offer was presented at three price points and declined at all three. No payment, agreement or onboarding step was reachable.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete run of the money play in this batch. Isolation ran ('finances aside, do you genuinely feel that the money is the only thing that's in a way for you'), the should/how reframe ran, the permission question ran and was granted ('let's have an open conversation about it, if you are open to it'), the nature of the constraint was clarified ('when you say you cannot afford it, is it you don't have the exact whole amount or is it like, what exactly do you mean?'), and the break-it-up option was offered, unlike on this rep's other two calls the same day. The financial picture came back nearly complete: income structure, alimony percentage, child support, take-home, rent, utilities and monthly surplus. Missing from the script: number of credit cards, total available credit, used versus available, and investments. Two things went wrong despite the coverage. The challenge frame — 'when someone says cannot afford it, but actually it turns out that hey, actually I can afford it, but I'm just scared to pull the trigger' — was deployed before the numbers were known and was flatly rebutted with real figures. And the play has no stopping condition: once the prospect had demonstrated the constraint was real and stated it was also a willingness boundary, the correct move was to disqualify, and instead an unauthorised tier was invented.

Triggered by 'this is something that I'm going to have to think about'. Two moves ran in substance — 'Earlier, you mentioned you were confident about this actually could work for you, right?' maps to the can-it-get-you-there move, and 'help me understand, apart from the price, what's changed between then and now?' maps to what's-actually-coming-up. None of the deciding-versus-thinking moves, the different-decision frame, or the identity question ran. The prospect's answer was honest and complete — 'No, nothing's changed. It's just the price. It's a sticker shock' — which correctly closed the play out as a price problem rather than a thinking problem.

Clinical fit, and the most serious instance in the corpus so far. The prospect disclosed an explicit and current clinician restriction on overhead loading, plus scheduled cortisone injections for suspected bilateral shoulder tears. There is no scripted screening or clearance step. Worse than an omission, the gap was filled with a counter-claim: 'with kettlebell training, it is joint friendly and it's joint friendly by design... the movement patterns strengthen the shoulder complex instead of grinding it down.' A separately disclosed new blood pressure elevation from a 110 baseline to 130-140 was never returned to at all.

A prospect with demonstrated, arithmetically verified absence of capacity who has also stated it is a willingness boundary. The playbook's money play assumes hidden capacity and offers no exit when capacity is genuinely absent. There is no disqualification move, no graceful close, and no defined lower-priced product to route to. The rep filled the vacuum by inventing a $4,000 three-month tier and then pushing consumer credit three times after explicit refusals — a script gap producing rep behaviour nobody would sanction if asked directly.

notes: Discovery here is the strongest in the batch and should be used for training — the hereditary probe, the double-pass injury questioning, and the drive from a shrugged 'it would be nice to be lean' through to his father on the floor and his step-grandfather's amputated leg. Everything that went wrong went wrong after the price. Three corrections. First and non-negotiable: when a prospect states that his surgeon has restricted overhead loading, the call stops and the question becomes whether the surgeon will clear this, not whether the product is joint-friendly. Second, a conditional yes at P6c is information — 'if this is something that I can afford' needed a question, not a price. Third, the money play needs a stopping rule; this prospect gave complete numbers proving the constraint was real, and continuing past that produced an invented tier and three refused credit pushes rather than a clean, respectful disqualification of someone who would have been a good client in eighteen months.
